text: The photographs are the business: women bared and flogged, arranged for the lens, printed and sold quietly into the parlors of respectable Petersburg. Aleksei Balabanov sets this in the first years of the last century, when a camera was still a machine with a technician attached, and the technician worked in rooms nobody admitted visiting. Johann keeps his own counsel; his assistants keep busy; and the trade moves inward from studio to household until two well-off families have arranged their week around a supplier they would not name aloud. It is filed as comedy as well as drama, and that is no error: the manners hold long after everything beneath them has given way. A European Film Award for Best Actress came out of that stillness. Ninety-three minutes, and no hurry in any of them.

Every notice of his acting is a courtesy paid to his father's name. Kikunosuke Onoue performs women's roles on a Tokyo stage in the last years of the nineteenth century, adopted into an established acting family and applauded on credit, and when he learns what the audience actually thinks, the discovery sends him toward Otoku, a servant in the household. They fall in love. He decides to build a reputation somewhere the surname means nothing, and she goes with him. Kenji Mizoguchi, filming in 1939, gives a hundred and forty-four minutes to what comes after that decision: small troupes, provincial halls, a name that opens no doors. The subject turns out to be the arithmetic of it — who pays, and in what currency, for an artist's second attempt at being taken seriously.

Masuria after the war: the border has been drawn again across the farm, and the woman still working it was married to a German soldier who did not come back. That is Rose's whole position — a house, a field, and a marriage that suits nobody's side of the new arrangement. Russian troops passing through treat her as an account left open. Poles arriving with nothing see land. Then Tadeusz turns up, a Home Army officer who walked away from his own war and travels now under a false version of himself, and stays. At home the film was voted the country's best of its year, which suggests what Poland was prepared to sit through: ninety minutes in which help and self-interest are the same gesture, and no one in the house can afford to say so.

The philosopher in this house is the cat, and he argues with the rabbi in a voice nobody asked for. He is fluent, unkind, and openly attached to the man's teenage daughter, which makes the household a running negotiation rather than a fable. Comedy here is largely a matter of who gets to interrupt whom, and the cat interrupts everyone. Antoine Delesvaux plays it straight as domestic argument — doctrine debated at eye level by an animal with no interest in being respectable — and animation is what permits it, since a cat can say at that table what a person could not. Annecy handed it the Cristal. What lasts is smaller than the prize: a rabbi obliged, repeatedly, to work out whether a creature that has learned to speak is therefore a creature that must behave.

Two locomotives set out along the same stretch of Siberian track, and the men driving them have agreed to call it a race. This is the hinterland just after the Second World War, a settlement of Russians and Germans whose papers and histories have been shuffled together, and Alexey Uchitel is drawn to the exchange that follows: victors slipping into the manner of the defeated, the defeated carrying themselves like men who won. Russia put the film forward for the Academy Awards that year. Ignat has the bearing of the soldier from the posters and the nerves of a man who has not been right in years. The engines have names. What the film offers him instead of treatment is a machine: steam, a length of track, and other people willing to stand near it.

Three hours and seven minutes, and the knot in the middle of it is a face: the girl has her mother's, and the man who loved her mother is still around to see it. Viren's feeling for Pallavi went nowhere in its own time — she married Siddharth — and it comes back to him a generation later attached to a young woman with her own will and no interest in being anyone's reminder. Yash Chopra works at the scale popular Hindi cinema of 1991 could still command, and spends it keeping the situation from collapsing into a joke: songs, distances, whole years falling between one scene and the next. Filmfare named it the year's best film. The discomfort at the center is deliberate, and the film never pretends otherwise; it simply keeps the two of them in the same rooms.

He has been working abroad for years, and he comes home for the holiday with a plan nobody at the table knows about. The gap between what Adam says he is home for and what he is actually there to arrange runs the whole hundred minutes, most of which are relatives in one room, eating, drinking, talking over each other. Piotr Domalewski lets it be funny, the way family occasions are funny until roughly the fourth hour. Underneath sits money: what comes back from abroad, who assumes a share of it, what a man owes the people he stayed away from. Christmas supplies the clock — everyone is stuck in the same rooms for as long as the occasion lasts. The decisive conversation happens in a kitchen, sideways, while somebody hunts for a bottle opener.

Kai is a middle-school student who has decided in advance that nothing is going to happen to him. Then a mermaid arrives. Lu turns up in a fishing village where the adults settled long ago on what the sea is for and what a boy that age ought to want, and she has no working knowledge of either. The film is filed as a musical as much as an adventure, and that is the mechanism: it is built to move rather than explain, feeling arriving as sound and motion before anyone locates a word for it. Annecy's Cristal, the festival's feature prize, went to it. Masaaki Yuasa's real subject is the embarrassment of being that age in a small town, and what becomes of it when something turns up that has no idea what embarrassment is.

The year Stalin died, the camps let people out — and not mainly the ones who had been sent there for talking. The amnesty reaches a settlement remote enough that its defense consists of whoever happens to live there, plus two political exiles the state has already finished with. The men arriving have no politics at all, only appetite. Aleksandr Proshkin films it in the shape of a western: an isolated place, a handful of people, one road in and nothing coming down it. It was made in the Soviet Union in 1988, with the year in its title thirty-five years behind it, and the Nika went to it as best picture. What it is actually weighing is the position of two men punished for what they thought, now expected to stand between the settlement and that road.

A conviction costs nothing until it costs a house, a job, and the children. The student is accused of killing a policeman; the professor who takes her side is married, employed, and about to be neither. Per Fly follows the leaving rather than the case: the phone calls, the money, the colleagues who stop returning messages, the children handed a version of events. Her politics are her own; his arrive with her, late, and the film keeps pressing on that difference — what an opinion costs a comfortable man once it is attached to one particular person facing one particular charge. Denmark, 2005, and the trouble is domestic long before it is legal. A European Film Award for Best Actor came out of it, which figures, since most of this happens in a face.

Her parents built her a world and she lives in it without complaint; his family made no such arrangements for him. Both are Jewish, both American, and the distance that matters runs between the two households rather than between the two of them. They meet, they like each other, and the liking is the last simple thing available — every conversation after it turns out to be about competing ideas of what a family is owed. Larry Peerce lets the dialogue carry the weight, and the Academy gave the adapted screenplay its award; the film earns that in scenes where the thing at issue goes unsaid and lands anyway. 1969 is late enough for the affair to be shown for what it is. The comedy is genuine, and so is the draft of cold air under it.

The rift opens while the son is still a child, and nothing either of them does afterward closes it. The father is a policeman; the boy grows into the trade his father spends his working life against, which means every professional decision one of them takes arrives at home as a personal one. Ramesh Sippy runs a hundred and sixty-five minutes at the scale popular Hindi cinema of 1982 could command, and uses it for something narrower than a crime picture: two men in one family who cannot stop being what they are in front of each other. It took Filmfare's best film award that year. The action is there and it moves, but the film keeps returning to a room where the two of them have to sit.
